metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: How much is in the gene and how much is in the experience

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: of an individual.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Obviously, it's both that play a role

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and I believe that the way evolution gives,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: put prior information, so to speak, hardware,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: it's not really hardware,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: but that's essentially an hypothesis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I think what's going on is that evolution

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: as almost necessarily if you believe in Darwin

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: is very opportunistic and think about our DNA

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and the DNA of Drosophila,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: our DNA does not have many more genes than Drosophila.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The fly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The fly, the fruit fly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Now we know that the fruit fly does not learn very much

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: during its individual existence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It looks like one of these machinery

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: that it's really mostly not 100%,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: but 95% hard-coded by the genes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But since we don't have many more genes than Drosophila,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: evolution could encode in as a kind of general learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: machinery and then had to give very weak priors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Like for instance, let me give a specific example,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: which is recent work by a member of our Center for Brains,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Minds and Machines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: We know because of work of other people in our group

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and other groups that there are cells in a part of our brain,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: neurons that are tuned to faces.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: They seems to be involved in face recognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Now this face area exists,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: seems to be present in young children and adults.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And one question is, is there from the beginning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: is hardwired by evolution or somehow is learned very quickly?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So what's your, by the way, a lot of the questions I'm asking,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: the answer is we don't really know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But as a person who has contributed some profound ideas

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: in these fields, you're a good person to guess at some of these.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So of course, there's a caveat before a lot of the stuff we talk about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But what is your hunch?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Is the face, the part of the brain that seems to be concentrated

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: on face recognition, are you born with that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Or you just is designed to learn that quickly,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: like the face of the mother and so on?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: My hunch, my bias was the second one, learned very quickly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And it turns out that Marge Livingston at Harvard

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: has done some amazing experiments in which she raised baby monkeys,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: depriving them of faces during the first weeks of life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So they see technicians, but the technician have a mask.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And so when they looked at the area in the brain of these monkeys

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: that usually find faces, they found no face preference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So my guess is that what evolution does in this case is there is a plastic,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: an area which is plastic, which is kind of predetermined

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: to be imprinted very easily.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But the command from the gene is not a detailed circuitry

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: for a face template.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Could be, but this will require probably a lot of bits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You have to specify a lot of connections,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: a lot of neurons.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Instead, the command from the gene is something like imprint,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: memorize what you see most often in the first two weeks of life,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: especially in connection with food and maybe nipples.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Right. Well, source of food.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And so that area is very plastic at first and then solidifies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It'd be interesting if a variant of that experiment would show a different

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: kind of pattern associated with food than a face pattern,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: whether that could stick.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: There are indications that during that experiment,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: what the monkeys saw quite often were the blue gloves of the technicians

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: that were giving to the baby monkeys the milk.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And some of the cells, instead of being face sensitive in that area,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: are hand sensitive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Can you talk about what are the different parts of the brain

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and in your view sort of loosely and how do they contribute to intelligence?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you see the brain as a bunch of different modules

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and they together come in the human brain to create intelligence

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: or is it all one mush of the same kind of fundamental

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: architecture?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yeah, that's an important question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And there was a phase in neuroscience back in the 1950s or so

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: in which it was believed for a while that the brain was equipotential.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: This was the term.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You could cut out a piece and you could cut out a piece

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and nothing special happened apart from a little bit less performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: There was a surgeon, Lashley, who did a lot of experiments of this type

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: with mice and rats and concluded that every part of the brain

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: was essentially equivalent to any other one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It turns out that that's really not true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: There are very specific modules in the brain, as you said,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and people may lose the ability to speak if you have a stroke

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: in a certain region or may lose control of their legs in another region.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So they're very specific.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The brain is also quite flexible and redundant, so often it can correct things

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and take over functions from one part of the brain to the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But really there are specific modules.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So the answer that we know from this old work, which was basically based on lesions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: either on animals or very often there was a mine of very interesting data

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: coming from the war, from different types of injuries that soldiers had in the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: More recently, functional MRI, which allow you to check which parts of the brain

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: are active when you are doing different tasks, can replace some of this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You can see that certain parts of the brain are involved, are active.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: In vision, language, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Taking a step back to that part of the brain that specializes in the face

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and how that might be learned, what's your intuition behind?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Is it possible that from a physicist's perspective, when you get lower and lower,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: it's all the same stuff and when you're born it's plastic and quickly figures out

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: this part is going to be about vision, this is going to be about language,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: this is about common sense reasoning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you have an intuition that that kind of learning is going on really quickly

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: or is it really kind of solidified in hardware?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's a great question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: There are parts of the brain like the cerebellum or the hippocampus

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: that are quite different from each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: They clearly have different anatomy, different connectivity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Then there is the cortex, which is the most developed part of the brain in humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: In the cortex, you have different regions of the cortex that are responsible for vision,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: for audition, for motor control, for language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Now, one of the big puzzles of this is that the cortex is the cortex,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: it looks like it is the same in terms of hardware,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: in terms of type of neurons and connectivity across these different modalities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: For the cortex, I think aside these other parts of the brain like spinal cord,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: hippocampus, cerebellum and so on, for the cortex, I think your question about hardware

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and software and learning and so on, I think it's rather open.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I find it very interesting for us to think about an architecture, computer architecture,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: that is good for vision and at the same time is good for language.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It seems to be so different problem areas that you have to solve.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But the underlying mechanism might be the same and that's really instructive for artificial neural networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So you've done a lot of great work in vision, in human vision, computer vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You mentioned the problem of human vision is really as difficult as the problem of general intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Maybe that connects to the cortex discussion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Can you describe the human visual cortex and how the humans begin to understand the world

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: through the raw sensory information?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: What's, for folks enough, familiar, especially on the computer vision side,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: we don't often actually take a step back except saying with a sentence or two that one is inspired by the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: What is it that we know about the human visual cortex? That's interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: We know quite a bit. At the same time, we don't know a lot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But the bit we know, in a sense, we know a lot of the details and many we don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And we know a lot of the top level, the answer to the top level question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But we don't know some basic ones, even in terms of general neuroscience for getting vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Why do we sleep? It's such a basic question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And we really don't have an answer to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you think, so taking a step back on that, so sleep, for example, is fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you think that's a neuroscience question?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Or if we talk about abstractions, what do you think is an interesting way to study intelligence

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: or most effective on the levels of abstraction? Is it chemical? Is it biological?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Is it electrophysical, mathematical, as you've done a lot of excellent work on that side?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Which psychology, sort of like at which level of abstraction do you think?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Well, in terms of levels of abstraction, I think we need all of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It's like if you ask me, what does it mean to understand a computer?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's much simpler. But in a computer, I could say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: well, I understand how to use PowerPoint.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's my level of understanding a computer. It is reasonable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It gives me some power to produce slides and beautiful slides.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Now, you can ask somebody else, he says, well, I know how the transistors work that are inside the computer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I can write the equation for transistors and diodes and circuits, logical circuits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And I can ask this guy, do you know how to operate PowerPoint? No idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So do you think if we discovered computers walking amongst us,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: full of these transistors that are also operating under windows and have PowerPoint,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: do you think it's digging in a little bit more?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: How useful is it to understand the transistor in order to be able to understand

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: PowerPoint and these higher level intelligent processes?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So I think in the case of computers, because they were made by engineers, by us,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: this different level of understanding are rather separate on purpose.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: They are separate modules so that the engineer that designed the circuit for the chips

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: does not need to know what is inside PowerPoint.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Somebody can write the software translating from one to the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So in that case, I don't think understanding the transistor help you understand PowerPoint or very little.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: If you want to understand the computer, this question, I would say you have to understand it at different levels.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: If you really want to build one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But for the brain, I think these levels of understanding, so the algorithms,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: which kind of computation, the equivalent of PowerPoint and the circuits, the transistors,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I think they are much more intertwined with each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: There is not a neatly level of the software separate from the hardware.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And so that's why I think in the case of the brain, the problem is more difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: More than for computers, it requires the interaction, the collaboration between different types of expertise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The brain is a big hierarchical mess. You can't just disentangle levels.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I think you can, but it's much more difficult and it's not completely obvious.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And as I said, I think it's one of the, personally, I think it's the greatest problem in science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So I think it's fair that it's difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's a difficult one. That said, you do talk about compositionality and why it might be useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And when you discuss why these neural networks in artificial or biological sense learn anything,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: you talk about compositionality, there's a sense that nature can be disentangled.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: All aspects of our cognition could be disentangled to some degree.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So why do you think, first of all, how do you see compositionality and why do you think it exists at all in nature?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I spoke about, I used the term compositionality when we looked at deep neural networks,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: multilayers, and trying to understand when and why they are more powerful than more classical one-layer networks

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: like linear classifier, kernel machines, so-called.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And what we found is that in terms of approximating or learning or representing a function,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: a mapping from an input to an output, like from an image to the label in the image,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: if this function has a particular structure, then deep networks are much more powerful than shallow networks

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: to approximate the underlying function. And the particular structure is a structure of compositionality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: If the function is made up of functions of functions, so that you need to look on,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: when you are interpreting an image, classifying an image, you don't need to look at all pixels at once,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: but you can compute something from small groups of pixels,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and then you can compute something on the output of this local computation and so on,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: which is similar to what you do when you read a sentence. You don't need to read the first and the last letter,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: but you can read syllables, combine them in words, combine the words in sentences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So this is this kind of structure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So that's part of the discussion of why deep neural networks may be more effective than the shallow methods.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And is your sense for most things we can use neural networks for,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: those problems are going to be compositional in nature, like language, like vision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: How far can we get in this kind of way?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So here is almost philosophy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Well, let's go there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yeah, let's go there. So a friend of mine, Max Tegmark, who is a physicist at MIT.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I've talked to him on this thing. Yeah, and he disagrees with you, right? A little bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You know, we agree on most, but the conclusion is a bit different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: His conclusion is that for images, for instance, the compositional structure of this function that we have to learn

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: or to solve these problems comes from physics, comes from the fact that you have local interactions

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: in physics between atoms and other atoms, between particle of matter and other particles,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: between planets and other planets, between stars and others. It's all local.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And that's true. But you could push this argument a bit further.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Not this argument, actually. You could argue that maybe that's part of the truth,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: but maybe what happens is kind of the opposite, is that our brain is wired up as a deep network.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So it can learn, understand, solve problems that have this compositional structure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And it cannot do, it cannot solve problems that don't have this compositional structure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So the problem is we are accustomed to, we think about, we test our algorithms on,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: are these compositional structures because our brain is made up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And that's, in a sense, an evolutionary perspective that we've...

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The ones that weren't dealing with the compositional nature of reality died off.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yes, but also could be maybe the reason why we have this local connectivity in the brain,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: like simple cells in cortex looking only at the small part of the image, each one of them,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and then other cells looking at the small number of these simple cells and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The reason for this may be purely that it was difficult to grow long-range connectivity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So suppose it's, you know, for biology, it's possible to grow short-range connectivity,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: but not long-range also because there is a limited number of long-range that you can...

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And so you have this limitation from the biology, and this means you build a deep convolutional network.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: This would be something like a deep convolutional network.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And this is great for solving certain class of problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: These are the ones we find easy and important for our life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And yes, they were enough for us to survive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And you can start a successful business on solving those problems, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Like with mobile eye, driving is a compositional problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So on the learning task, I mean, we don't know much about how the brain learns in terms of optimization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But so the thing that's stochastic gradient descent is what artificial neural networks use for the most part to...

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Adjust the parameters in such a way that it's able to deal based on the label data, it's able to solve the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So what's your intuition about why it works at all?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: How hard of a problem it is to optimize a neural network, artificial neural network?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Is there other alternatives?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Just in general, your intuition is behind this very simplistic algorithm that seems to do pretty good, surprisingly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So I find neuroscience, the architecture of cortex is really similar to the architecture of deep networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So there is a nice correspondence there between the biology and this kind of local connectivity, hierarchical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Architecture, the stochastic gradient descent, as you said, is a very simple technique.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It seems pretty unlikely that biology could do that from what we know right now about cortex and neurons and synapses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So it's a big question open whether there are other optimization learning algorithms that can replace stochastic gradient descent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And my guess is yes, but nobody has found yet a real answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I mean, people are trying, still trying, and there are some interesting ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The fact that stochastic gradient descent is so successful, this has become clearly not so mysterious.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And the reason is that it's an interesting fact, you know, is a change in a sense in how people think about statistics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And this is the following, is that typically when you had data and you had, say, a model with parameters,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: you are trying to fit the model to the data, you know, to fit the parameter.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Typically, the kind of crowd wisdom type idea was you should have at least twice the number of data than the number of parameters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Maybe 10 times is better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Now, the way you train neural network these days is that they have 10 or 100 times more parameters than data, exactly the opposite.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And which, you know, it has been one of the puzzles about neural networks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: How can you get something that really works when you have so much freedom?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: From that little data, it can generalize somehow.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Right, exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you think the stochastic nature of it is essential, the randomness?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So I think we have some initial understanding why this happens.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But one nice side effect of having this overparameterization, more parameters than data,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: is that when you look for the minima of a loss function, like stochastic gradient descent is doing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: you find I made some calculations based on some old basic theorem of algebra called the Bezout theorem

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: that gives you an estimate of the number of solutions of a system of polynomial equations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Anyway, the bottom line is that there are probably more minima for a typical deep networks than atoms in the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Just to say there are a lot because of the overparameterization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: More global minimum, zero minimum, good minimum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: More global minima.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: A lot of them. So you have a lot of solutions. So it's not so surprising that you can find them relatively easily.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: This is because of the overparameterization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The overparameterization sprinkles that entire space with solutions that are pretty good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It's not so surprising.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It's like if you have a system of linear equations and you have more unknowns than equations,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: then you have, we know you have an infinite number of solutions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And the question is to pick one. That's another story.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But you have an infinite number of solutions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So there are a lot of value of your unknowns that satisfy the equations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But it's possible that there's a lot of those solutions that aren't very good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: What's surprising is that they're pretty good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So that's a question. Why can you pick one that generalizes well?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's a separate question with separate answers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: One theorem that people like to talk about that kind of inspires imagination of the power of neural networks

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: is the universal approximation theorem that you can approximate any computable function

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: with just a finite number of neurons in a single hidden layer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you find this theorem one surprising? Do you find it useful, interesting, inspiring?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: No, this one, I never found it very surprising.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It was known since the 80s since I entered the field because it's basically the same as Weierstrass theorem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: which says that I can approximate any continuous function with a polynomial of sufficiently,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: with a sufficient number of terms, monomials.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It's basically the same and the proofs are very similar.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So your intuition was there was never any doubt that neural networks in theory could be very strong approximators.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The question, the interesting question is that if this theorem says you can approximate, fine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But when you ask how many neurons, for instance, or in the case of polynomial,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: many monomials, I need to get a good approximation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Then it turns out that that depends on the dimensionality of your function, how many variables you have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But it depends on the dimensionality of your function in a bad way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It's for instance, suppose you want an error which is no worse than 10 percent in your approximation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You come up with a network that approximates your function within 10 percent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Then turns out that the number of units you need are in the order of 10 to the dimensionality, D, how many variables.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So if you have two variables, these two, you have 100 units and okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But if you have, say, 200 by 200 pixel images, now this is 40,000, whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: We again go to the size of the universe pretty quickly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Exactly, 10 to the 40,000 or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And so this is called the curse of dimensionality, not quite appropriate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And the hope is with the extra layers you can remove the curse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: What we proved is that if you have deep layers, hierarchical architecture with local connectivity

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: of the type of convolutional deep learning, and if you're dealing with a function that has this kind of hierarchical architecture,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: then you avoid completely the curse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You've spoken a lot about supervised deep learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: What are your thoughts, hopes, views on the challenges of unsupervised learning with GANs,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: with Generative Adversarial Networks?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you see those as distinct, the power of GANs, do you see those as distinct from supervised methods in neural networks,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: or are they really all in the same representation ballpark?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: GANs is one way to get estimation of probability densities,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: which is a somewhat new way that people have not done before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I don't know whether this will really play an important role in intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It's interesting. I'm less enthusiastic about it than many people in the field.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I have the feeling that many people in the field are really impressed by the ability of producing realistic-looking images in this generative way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Which describes the popularity of the methods, but you're saying that while that's exciting and cool to look at,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: it may not be the tool that's useful for it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So you describe it beautifully. Current supervised methods go n to infinity in terms of the number of labeled points,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: and we really have to figure out how to go to n to 1.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And you're thinking GANs might help, but they might not be the right...

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I don't think for that problem, which I really think is important, they certainly have applications, for instance, in computer graphics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I did work long ago, which was a little bit similar in terms of saying,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I have a network and I present images, so input is images, and output is, for instance, the pose of the image.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: A face, how much is smiling, is rotated 45 degrees or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: What about having a network that I train with the same data set, but now I invert input and output.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Now the input is the pose or the expression, a number, certain numbers, and the output is the image, and I train it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And we did pretty good, interesting results in terms of producing very realistic-looking images.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It was a less sophisticated mechanism, but the output was pretty less than GANs, but the output was pretty much of the same quality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So I think for computer graphics type application, yeah, definitely GANs can be quite useful, and not only for that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: but for helping, for instance, on this problem of unsupervised example, reducing the number of labeled examples,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I think people, it's like they think they can get out more than they put in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: There's no free lunches, you said.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: What's your intuition, how can we slow the growth of N to infinity in supervised learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So, for example, Mobileye has very successfully, I mean essentially annotated large amounts of data to be able to drive a car.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Now one thought is, so we're trying to teach machines, School of AI, and we're trying to, so how can we become better teachers, maybe?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's one way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I like that, because again, one caricature of the history of computer sites, you could say, begins with programmers, expensive.

body.input: Continuous labelers, cheap.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And the future will be schools, like we have for kids.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yeah, currently the labeling methods were not selective about which examples we teach networks with.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So I think the focus of making networks that learn much faster is often on the architecture side,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: but how can we pick better examples with which to learn?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you have intuitions about that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's part of the problem, but the other one is, if we look at biology, a reasonable assumption, I think, is in the same spirit that I said,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: evolution is opportunistic and has weak priors. The way I think the intelligence of a child, the baby may develop is by bootstrapping weak priors from evolution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: For instance, you can assume that you have in most organisms, including human babies, built in some basic machinery to detect motion and relative motion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And in fact, there is, you know, we know all insects from fruit flies to other animals, they have this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Even in the retinas, in the very peripheral part, it's very conserved across species, something that evolution discovered early.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It may be the reason why babies tend to look in the first few days to moving objects and not to not moving objects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Now, moving objects means, okay, they're attracted by motion, but motion also means that motion gives automatic segmentation from the background.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So because of motion boundaries, either the object is moving or the eye of the baby is tracking the moving object and the background is moving.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yeah. So just purely on the visual characteristics of the scene, that seems to be the most useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Right. So it's like looking at an object without background.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: It's ideal for learning the object. Otherwise, it's really difficult because you have so much stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So suppose you do this at the beginning, first weeks, then after that you can recognize object.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Now they're imprinted, the number one, even in the background, even without motion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So that's it. By the way, I just want to ask on the object recognition problem. So there is this being responsive to movement and doing edge detection, essentially.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: What's the gap between being effectively effective at visually recognizing stuff, detecting where it is and understanding the scene?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Is this a huge gap in many layers or is it close?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: No, I think that's a huge gap. I think present algorithm with all the success that we have and the fact that are a lot of very useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I think we are in a golden age for applications of low level vision and low level speech recognition and so on, Alexa and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: There are many more things of similar level to be done, including medical diagnosis and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But we are far from what we call understanding of a scene, of language, of actions, of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That is, despite the claims, that's, I think, very far.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: We're a little bit off. So in popular culture and among many researchers, some of which I've spoken with, the Sue Russell and Elon Musk, in and out of the AI field, there's a concern about the existential threat of AI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So worry is good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: But ideally, at some point, we'll have an understanding of how this works and why it evolved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The big why question. Yeah, it must have some some purpose.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yeah, obviously, it has some social purposes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Probably if neuroscience holds the key to at least eliminate some aspect of ethics, that means it could be a learnable problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yeah, exactly. And as we're getting into harder and harder questions, let's go to the hard problem of consciousness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Is this an important problem for us to think about and solve on the engineering of intelligence side of your work, of our dream?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You know, it's unclear. So, you know, again, this is a deep problem, partly because it's very difficult to define consciousness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: And there is a debate among neuroscientists about whether consciousness and philosophers, of course,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: whether consciousness is something that requires flesh and blood, so to speak.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Or could be, you know, that we could have silicone devices that are conscious or up to statement,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: like everything has some degree of consciousness and some more than others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: This is like Giulio Tonioni and Fee.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: We just recently talked to Christophe Coq.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Christophe was my first graduate student.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you think it's important to illuminate aspects of consciousness in order to engineer intelligence systems?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you think an intelligence system would ultimately have consciousness? Are they interlinked?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You know, most of the people working in artificial intelligence, I think, would answer, we don't strictly need consciousness to have an intelligence system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: That's sort of the easier question because it's a very engineering answer to the question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Pass the Turing test, we don't need consciousness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you think it's possible that we need to have that kind of self-awareness?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: We may, yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: So, for instance, I personally think that when test a machine or a person in a Turing test, in an extended Turing test,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I think consciousness is part of what we require in that test, you know, implicitly to say that this is intelligent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Christophe disagrees.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yes, he does.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Despite many other romantic notions he holds, he disagrees with that one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yes, that's right. So, you know, we'll see.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you think, as a quick question, Ernest Becker's Fear of Death,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: do you think mortality and those kinds of things are important for, well, for consciousness and for intelligence?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: The finiteness of life, finiteness of existence?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Or is that just a side effect of evolutionary side effects that's useful for natural selection?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Do you think this kind of thing that this interview is going to run out of time soon, our life will run out of time soon,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: do you think that's needed to make this conversation good and life good?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You know, I never thought about it. It's a very interesting question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: I think Steve Jobs in his commencement speech at Stanford argued that, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: having a finite life was important for stimulating achievements. It was a different...

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: You live every day like it's your last, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yeah, yeah. So, rationally, I don't think strictly you need mortality for consciousness, but...

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Who knows? They seem to go together in our biological system, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

body.input: Yeah, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13

metadata.title: Podcast: Tomaso Poggio: Brains, Minds, and Machines | Lex Fridman Podcast #13
