body.input: you know, to what extent, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: gods can be made manifest in the physical world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I'm not sure my colleagues would like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So let's talk about quantum computers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yeah, sure, sure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: As you've said, quantum computing, at least in the 1990s,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: was a profound story at the intersection of computer science,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: physics, engineering, math, and philosophy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So there's this broad and deep aspect to quantum computing

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that represents more than just the quantum computer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But can we start at the very basics?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: What is quantum computing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yeah, so it's a proposal for a new type of computation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: or let's say a new way to harness nature to do computation

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that is based on the principles of quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay, now the principles of quantum mechanics

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: have been in place since 1926.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You know, they haven't changed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You know, what's new is, you know, how we want to use them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay, so what does quantum mechanics say about the world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You know, the physicists, I think, over the generations,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you know, convinced people that that is an unbelievably complicated question

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and, you know, just give up on trying to understand it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I can let you in, not being a physicist, I can let you in on a secret,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: which is that it becomes a lot simpler if you do what we do

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: in quantum information theory and sort of take the physics out of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So the way that we think about quantum mechanics

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: is sort of as a generalization of the rules of probability themselves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So, you know, you might say there was a 30% chance

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that it was going to snow today or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You would never say that there was a negative 30% chance, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That would be nonsense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Much less would you say that there was an I% chance,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you know, a square root of minus 1% chance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Now, the central discovery that sort of quantum mechanics made

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: is that fundamentally the world is described by, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: the sort of, let's say, the possibilities for, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: what a system could be doing are described using numbers called amplitudes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: okay, which are like probabilities in some ways,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: but they are not probabilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: They can be positive, for one thing, they can be positive or negative.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: In fact, they can even be complex numbers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay, and if you've heard of a quantum superposition,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: this just means that some state of affairs

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: where you assign an amplitude, one of these complex numbers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: to every possible configuration

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that you could see a system in on measuring it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So, for example, you might say that an electron has some amplitude

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: for being here and some other amplitude for being there, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Now, if you look to see where it is, you will localize it, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You will sort of force the amplitudes to be converted into probabilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That happens by taking their squared absolute value, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And then, you know, you can say either the electron will be here

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: or it will be there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And, you know, knowing the amplitudes, you can predict at least the probabilities

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that you'll see each possible outcome, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But while a system is isolated from the whole rest of the universe,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: the rest of its environment, the amplitudes can change in time

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: by rules that are different from the normal rules of probability

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and that are, you know, alien to our everyday experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So, anytime anyone ever tells you anything about the weirdness of the quantum world,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you know, or assuming that they're not lying to you, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: They are telling you, you know, yet another consequence of nature

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: being described by these amplitudes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So, most famously, what amplitudes can do is that they can interfere with each other, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So, in the famous double slit experiment, what happens is that you shoot a particle,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: like an electron, let's say, at a screen with two slits in it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and you find that there are, you know, on a second screen,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: now there are certain places where that electron will never end up,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you know, after it passes through the first screen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And yet, if I close off one of the slits, then the electron can appear in that place, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So, by decreasing the number of paths that the electron could take to get somewhere,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you can increase the chance that it gets there, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Now, how is that possible?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Well, it's because, you know, as we would say now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: the electron has a superposition state, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: It has some amplitude for reaching this point by going through the first slit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: It has some other amplitude for reaching it by going through the second slit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But now, if one amplitude is positive and the other one is negative,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: then I have to add them all up, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I have to add the amplitudes for every path that the electron could have taken to reach this point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And those amplitudes, if they're pointing in different directions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: they can cancel each other out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That would mean the total amplitude is zero and the thing never happens at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I close off one of the possibilities, then the amplitude is positive or it's negative,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and now the thing can't happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay, so that is sort of the one trick of quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And now, I can tell you what a quantum computer is, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: A quantum computer is a computer that tries to exploit, you know, these,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: exactly these phenomena, superposition, amplitudes, and interference

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: in order to solve certain problems much faster than we know how to solve them otherwise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So, it's the basic building block of a quantum computer is what we call a quantum bit or a qubit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That just means a bit that has some amplitude for being zero and some other amplitude for being one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So, it's a superposition of zero and one states, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But now, the key point is that if I've got, let's say, a thousand qubits,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: the rules of quantum mechanics are completely unequivocal

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that I do not just need one amplitude, you know, I don't just need amplitudes for each qubit separately.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay, in general, I need an amplitude for every possible setting of all thousand of those bits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay, so that what that means is two to the one thousand power amplitudes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay, if I had to write those down, let's say in the memory of a conventional computer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: if I had to write down two to the one thousand complex numbers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that would not fit within the entire observable universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay, and yet, you know, quantum mechanics is unequivocal that if these qubits can all interact with each other,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and in some sense, I need two to the one thousand parameters, you know, amplitudes to describe what is going on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Now, you know, now I can tell you where all the popular articles, you know, about quantum computing go off the rails

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: is that they say, you know, they sort of say what I just said, and then they say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: oh, so the way a quantum computer works is just by trying every possible answer in parallel.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You know, that sounds too good to be true, and unfortunately, it kind of is too good to be true.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: The problem is I could make a superposition over every possible answer to my problem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you know, even if there were two to the one thousand of them, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I can easily do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: The trouble is for a computer to be useful, you've got at some point, you've got to look at it and see an output,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: right? And if I just measure a superposition over every possible answer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: then the rules of quantum mechanics tell me that all I'll see will be a random answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You know, if I just wanted a random answer, well, I could have picked one myself with a lot less trouble, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So the entire trick with quantum computing, with every algorithm for a quantum computer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: is that you try to choreograph a pattern of interference of amplitudes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and you try to do it so that for each wrong answer, some of the paths leading to that wrong answer have positive amplitudes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and others have negative amplitudes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So on the whole, they cancel each other out, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Whereas all the paths leading to the right answer should reinforce each other, you know, should have amplitudes pointing the same direction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So the design of algorithms in this space is the choreography of the interferences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Precisely. That's precisely what it is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Can we take a brief step back and you mentioned information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So in which part of this beautiful picture that you've painted is information contained?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Oh, well, information is at the core of everything that we've been talking about, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I mean, the bit is, you know, the basic unit of information since, you know, Claude Shannon's paper in 1948,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you know, and, you know, of course, you know, people had the concept even before that, you know, he popularized the name, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But I mean, but a bit is zero or one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Basic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That's right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And what we would say is that the basic unit of quantum information is the qubit is, you know, the object,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: any object that can be maintained in this manipulated in a superposition of zero and one states.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Now, you know, sometimes people ask, well, but but but what is a qubit physically?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Right. And there are all these different, you know, proposals that are being pursued in parallel for how you implement qubits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: There is, you know, superconducting quantum computing that was in the news recently because of Google's quantum supremacy experiment, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Where you would have some little coils where a current can flow through them in two different energy states,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: one representing a zero, another representing the one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And if you cool these coils to just slightly above absolute zero, like a hundredth of a degree,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: then they superconduct and then the current can actually be in a superposition of the two different states.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So that's one kind of qubit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Another kind would be, you know, just an individual atomic nucleus, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: It has a spin.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: It could be spinning clockwise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: It could be spinning counterclockwise or it could be in a superposition of the two spin states.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That is another qubit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But just like in the classical world, you could be a virtuoso programmer without having any idea of what a transistor is, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Or how the bits are physically represented inside the machine, even that the machine uses electricity, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You just care about the logic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: It's sort of the same with quantum computing, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Qubits could be realized by many, many different quantum systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And yet all of those systems will lead to the same logic, you know, the logic of qubits and how you measure them, how you change them over time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so, you know, the subject of how qubits behave and what you can do with qubits, that is quantum information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So just to linger on that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So the physical design implementation of a qubit does not interfere with that next level of abstraction that you can program over it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So it truly is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: The idea of it is, is it OK?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Well, to be honest with you, today they do interfere with each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That's because all the quantum computers we can build today are very noisy, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so sort of the qubits are very far from perfect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so the lower level sort of does affect the higher levels and we sort of have to think about all of them at once.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: OK, but eventually where we hope to get is to what are called error corrected quantum computers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And in that future, you know, a future that we can already sort of prove theorems about or think about today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But in that future, the logic of it really does become decoupled from the hardware.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So if noise is currently like the biggest problem for quantum computing and then the dream is error correcting quantum computers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Absolutely. So, yes, the problem is even a little more specific than noise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So the fundamental problem, if you're trying to actually build a quantum computer of any appreciable size, is something called decoherence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: OK, and this was recognized from the very beginning when people first started thinking about this in the 1990s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: the state of your quantum computer and the external environment.

body.input: OK, and why is that such a problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Well, I talked before about how, you know, when you measure a quantum system,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: so let's say if I measure a qubit that's in a superposition of zero and one states to ask it, you know, are you zero or are you one?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Well, now I force it to make up its mind, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And now probabilistically, it chooses one or the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And now, you know, it's no longer a superposition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: There's no longer amplitudes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: There's just there's some probability that I get a zero and there's some that I get a one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And now the trouble is that it doesn't have to be me who's looking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: In fact, it doesn't have to be any conscious entity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Any kind of interaction with the external world that leaks out the information about whether this qubit was a zero or a one,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: sort of that causes the zero-ness or the one-ness of the qubit to be recorded in, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: the radiation in the room, in the molecules of the air, in the wires that are connected to my device, any of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: As soon as the information leaks out, it is as if that qubit has been measured.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: OK, it is, you know, the state has now collapsed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You know, another way to say it is that it's become entangled with its environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But, you know, from the perspective of someone who's just looking at this qubit, it is as though it has lost its quantum state.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so what this means is that if I want to do a quantum computation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I have to keep the qubits sort of fanatically well isolated from their environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But then at the same time, they can't be perfectly isolated because I need to tell them what to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I need to make them interact with each other, for one thing, and not only that, but in a precisely choreographed way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: OK, and, you know, that is such a staggering problem, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: How do I isolate these qubits from the whole universe, but then also tell them exactly what to do?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I mean, you know, there were distinguished physicists and computer scientists in the 90s who said this is fundamentally impossible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You know, the laws of physics will just never let you control qubits to the degree of accuracy that you're talking about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Now, what changed the views of most of us was a profound discovery in the mid to late 90s,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: which was called the theory of quantum error correction and quantum fault tolerance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: OK, and the upshot of that theory is that if I want to build a reliable quantum computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and scale it up to an arbitrary number of as many qubits as I want, you know, and doing as much on them as I want,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I do not actually have to get the qubits perfectly isolated from their environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: It is enough to get them really, really, really well isolated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: OK, and even if every qubit is sort of leaking its state into the environment at some rate,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: as long as that rate is low enough, I can sort of encode the information that I care about

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: in very clever ways across the collective states of multiple qubits in such a way that even if a small percentage of my qubits leak,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: well, I'm constantly monitoring them to see if that leak happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I can detect it and I can correct it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I can recover the information I care about from the remaining qubits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: OK, and so, you know, you can build a reliable quantum computer even out of unreliable parts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Right now, in some sense, you know, that discovery is what set the engineering agenda for quantum computing research from the 1990s until the present.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: but reliable enough that you can then use these error correcting codes to have them simulate qubits that are even more reliable than they are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So, you know, I don't think that that is, you know, coming soon,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: although people who have secrets that, you know, need to stay secret for 20 years, you know, are already worried about this,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you know, for the good reason that, you know, we presume that intelligence agencies are already scooping up data,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you know, in the hope that eventually they'll be able to decode it once quantum computers become available, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So this brings me to the second point I wanted to make,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: which is that there are other public key cryptosystems that are known

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that we don't know how to break even with quantum computers, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so there's a whole field devoted to this now, which is called post-quantum cryptography, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so there is already, so we have some good candidates now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: the best known being what are called lattice-based cryptosystems,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and there is already some push to try to migrate to these cryptosystems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So NIST in the US is holding a competition to create standards for post-quantum cryptography,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: which will be the first step in trying to get every web browser and every router to upgrade, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and use something like SSL that would be based on what we think is quantum secure cryptography.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But, you know, this will be a long process, but, you know, it is something that people are already starting to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so I'm sure this algorithm is sort of a dramatic discovery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You know, it could be a big deal for whatever intelligence agency first gets a scalable quantum computer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: at least certainly if no one else knows that they have it, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But eventually we think that we could migrate the internet to the post-quantum cryptography,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and then we'd be more or less back where we started, okay?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So this is sort of not the application of quantum computing, I think,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that's really going to change the world in a sustainable way, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: By the way, the biggest practical application of quantum computing that we know about by far,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I think, is simply the simulation of quantum mechanics itself

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: in order to learn about chemical reactions, design maybe new chemical processes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: new materials, new drugs, new solar cells, new superconductors, all kinds of things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: What's the size of a quantum computer that would be able to simulate the quantum mechanical systems themselves

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that would be impactful for the real world for the kind of chemical reactions and that kind of work?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: What scale are we talking about?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Now you're asking a very, very current question, a very big question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: People are going to be racing over the next decade to try to do useful quantum simulations,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: even with 100 or 200 qubit quantum computers of the sort that we expect to be able to build over the next decade.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That might be the first application of quantum computing that we're able to realize,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: or maybe it will prove to be too difficult, and maybe even that will require fault tolerance or will require error correction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So that's an aggressive race to come up with the one case study, kind of like with Peter Schor,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: with the idea that would just capture the world's imagination of, look, we can actually do something very useful here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yeah, but I think within the next decade, the best shot we have is certainly not using Schor's algorithm to break cryptography

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: just because it requires too much in the way of error correction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: The best shot we have is to do some quantum simulation that tells the material scientists or chemists or nuclear physicists

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: something that is useful to them and that they didn't already know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And you might only need one or two successes in order to change some billion-dollar industries.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: The way that people make fertilizer right now is still based on the Haber-Bosch process from a century ago,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: and it is some many-body quantum mechanics problem that no one really understands.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: If you could design a better way to make fertilizer, that's billions of dollars right there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So those are sort of the applications that people are going to be aggressively racing toward over the next decade.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Now, I don't know if they're going to realize it or not, but they certainly at least have a shot.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So it's going to be a very, very interesting next decade.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But just to clarify, what's your intuition?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Is it possible for that breakthrough to be on 50 to 100 qubits, or is scale a fundamental thing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: like 500, 1,000-plus qubits?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yeah. So I can tell you what the current studies are saying.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I think probably better to rely on that than on my intuition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But there was a group at Microsoft had a study a few years ago that said even with only about 100 qubits,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: you could already learn something new about the chemical reaction that makes fertilizer, for example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: The trouble is they're talking about 100 qubits and about a million layers of quantum gates.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So basically they're talking about 100 nearly perfect qubits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So the logical qubits, as you mentioned before.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yeah, exactly. 100 logical qubits.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And now the hard part for the next decade is going to be, well, what can we do with 100 to 200 noisy qubits?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yeah. Is there an error correction breakthrough that might come without the need to do thousands or millions of physical qubits?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yeah. So people are going to be pushing simultaneously on a bunch of different directions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: One direction, of course, is just making the qubits better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And there is tremendous progress there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I mean, the fidelity is like the accuracy of the qubits has improved by several orders of magnitude in the last decade or two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: The second thing is designing better, let's say, lower overhead error correcting codes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And even short of doing the full recursive error correction, there are these error mitigation strategies that you can use

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: that may allow you to eke out a useful speed up in the near term.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And then the third thing is just taking the quantum algorithms for simulating quantum chemistry or materials and making them more efficient.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And those algorithms are already dramatically more efficient than they were, let's say, five years ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so when I quoted these estimates like a circuit depth of one million,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I hope that because people will care enough that these numbers are going to come down.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So you're one of the world class researchers in this space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: There's a few groups I can mention, Google and IBM working at this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: There's other research labs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But you put also, you have an amazing blog.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You're too kind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You paid me to say it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You put a lot of effort sort of to communicating the science of this and communicating, exposing some of the BS and sort of the natural,

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: just like in the AI space, the natural charlatanism, if that's a word in this, in quantum mechanics in general, but quantum computers and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Can you give some notes about people or ideas that people like me or listeners in general from outside the field should be cautious of when they're taking in news headings that Google achieved quantum supremacy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So what should we look out for? Where's the charlatans in the space? Where's the BS?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yeah. So good question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Unfortunately, quantum computing is a little bit like cryptocurrency or deep learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: There is a core of something that is genuinely revolutionary and exciting.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And because of that core, it attracts this sort of vast penumbra of people making just utterly ridiculous claims.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so with quantum computing, I mean, I would say that the main way that people go astray is by not focusing on sort of the question of, are you getting a speed up over a classical computer or not?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so people have dismissed quantum supremacy because it's not useful or it's not itself, let's say, obviously useful for anything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay. But ironically, these are some of the same people who will go and say, well, we care about useful applications.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: We care about solving traffic routing and financial optimization and all these things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And that sounds really good, but their entire spiel is sort of counting on nobody asking the question, yes, but how well could a classical computer do the same thing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Right. I really mean the entire thing. They say, well, a quantum computer can do this, a quantum computer can do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And they just avoid the question, are you getting a speed up over a classical computer or not?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And if so, how do you know? Have you really thought carefully about classical algorithms to solve the same problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And a lot of the application areas that companies and investors are most excited about, that the popular press is most excited about for quantum computers have been things like machine learning, AI, optimization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay. And the problem with that is that since the very beginning, even if you have a perfect fault tolerant, scalable quantum computer, we have known of only modest speed ups that you can get for these problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay. So there is a famous quantum algorithm called Grover's algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay. And what it can do is it can solve many, many of the problems that arise in AI, machine learning, optimization, including NP complete problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay. But it can solve them in about the square root of the number of steps that a classical computer would need for the same problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay. Now a square root speed up is important. It's impressive. It is not an exponential speed up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay. So it is not the kind of game changer that let's say Shor's algorithm for factoring is, or for that matter, that simulation of quantum mechanics is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Okay. It is a more modest speed up. Let's say roughly, in theory, it could roughly double the size of the optimization problems that you could handle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Right. And so because people found that, I guess, too boring or too unimpressive, they've gone on to invent all of these heuristic algorithms where because no one really understands them, you can just project your hopes onto them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Right. That well, maybe it gets an exponential speed up. You can't prove that it doesn't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: You know, and the burden is on you to prove that it doesn't get a speed up. Right. And, you know, so they've done an immense amount of that kind of thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And a really worrying amount of the case for building a quantum computer has come to rest on this stuff that those of us in this field know perfectly well is on extremely shaky foundations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So the fundamental question is, show that there's a speed up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yes, absolutely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And in this space that you're referring to, which is actually interesting, the area that a lot of people excited about is machine learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So your sense is, do you think it will, I know that there's a lot of smoke currently, but do you think there actually eventually might be breakthroughs where you do get exponential speed ups in the machine learning space?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Absolutely, there might be. I mean, I think we know of modest speed ups that you can get for these problems. I think, you know, whether you can get bigger speed ups is one of the biggest questions for quantum computing theory, you know, for people like me to be thinking about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Now, you know, we had actually recently a really, you know, a super exciting candidate for an exponential quantum speed up for a machine learning problem that people really care about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: This is basically the Netflix problem, the problem of recommending products to users, given some sparse data about their preferences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Karenitas and Prakash in 2016 had an algorithm for sampling recommendations that was exponentially faster than any known classical algorithm, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so, you know, a lot of people were excited. I was excited about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I had an 18-year-old undergrad by the name of Yilin Tang, and she was, you know, she was obviously brilliant. She was looking for a project.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I gave her as a project, can you prove that this speed up is real? Can you prove that, you know, any classical algorithm would need to access exponentially more data, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And, you know, this was a case where if that was true, this was not like a P versus NP type of question, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: This might well have been provable, but she worked on it for a year. She couldn't do it. Eventually, she figured out why she couldn't do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And the reason was that that was false. There is a classical algorithm with a similar performance to the quantum algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: So Yilin succeeded in de-quantizing that machine learning algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And then in the last couple of years, building on Yilin's breakthrough, a bunch of the other quantum machine learning algorithms that were proposed have now also been de-quantized.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: That's a kind of important backwards step, or a forward step for science, but a step for quantum machine learning that precedes the big next forward step, if it's possible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Right. Now, some people will say, well, you know, there's a silver lining in this cloud.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: They say, well, thinking about quantum computing has led to the discovery of potentially useful new classical algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And so you get these spin-off applications. But if you want a quantum speed-up, you really have to think carefully about that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Yilin's work was a perfect illustration of why.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And I think that the challenge, the field is now open. Find a better example. Find where quantum computers are going to deliver big gains for machine learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And not only do I ardently support people thinking about that, I'm trying to think about it myself and have my students and post-docs think about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But we should not pretend that those speed-ups are already established.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And the problem comes when so many of the companies and journalists in this space are pretending that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Like all good things, like life itself, this conversation must soon come to an end.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Let me ask the most absurdly philosophical last question. What is the meaning of life?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: What gives your life fulfillment, purpose, happiness and meaning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I would say, number one, trying to discover new things about the world and share them and communicate and learn what other people have discovered.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Number two, my friends, my family, my kids, my students, the people around me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Number three, trying when I can to make the world better in some small ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: And it's depressing that I can't do more and that the world is facing crises over the climate and over sort of resurgent authoritarianism and all these other things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: But trying to stand against the things that I find horrible when I can.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Let me ask you one more absurd question. What makes you smile?

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Well, yeah, I guess your question just did. I don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: I thought I tried that absurd one on you. Well, it was a huge honor to talk to you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: We'll probably talk to you for many more hours. Scott, thank you so much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Well, thank you. Thank you. It was great.

metadata.title: Podcast: Scott Aaronson: Quantum Computing | Lex Fridman Podcast #72

body.input: Thank you for listening to this conversation with Scott Aronson.

body.input: The first group will tell you that only they possess the truth, and that the government will save you,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: the company will save you, the science, the authorities, the experts, the institutions will save you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: The second group, too, will tell you that only they possess the truth,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: and that the government will hurt you, the company will hurt you,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: the science, the authorities, the experts, the institutions will hurt you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Both groups have the benevolent and the malevolent, their heroes and their charlatans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: And I think the hard truth is that no one in this world can tell you with absolute certainty which is which.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: You have to use your mind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: This is the burden of being human, of being free.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Don't blindly follow any leader, neither the emperor nor the martyr who points out that the emperor has no clothes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: And then there's the lessons of history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Vaccines have saved hundreds of millions of lives in the past century,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: and in general, the advance of medicine has saved billions of lives.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: If you ignore the power of science, you're not being honest with the lessons of history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: And if you ignore the corrupting nature of power and money within institutions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: including governments and companies that led to the suffering and death of hundreds of millions in the past century,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: you are once again not being honest with the lessons of history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I announced that I will be having this conversation with Albert Berla,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Pfizer CEO, and a lot of people wrote to me, I would like to say that I was and am and always will be listening and learning with an open mind from everyone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: My own opinion, worth little as it is, is that the development of the COVID vaccines is one of the greatest accomplishments of science in recent history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: For the rest, from safety and efficacy to policy and economics, I stand humbled before a complicated world full of fear and anger.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: A small number of malicious people from all walks of life will use that fear and anger to divide us,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: because the division makes them money and gives them power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I took two shots of the Pfizer vaccine, this was my decision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I don't ever want to force this on anyone, and I certainly don't want to dismiss your concerns, or worse, you as a person if you choose not to get vaccinated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I can assure you one thing, in this conversation and in any conversation, the choice of questions I ask and words I say is mine and mine alone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: When my words fall short, as they often do, it is only because of the limitations of my mind and of my speaking ability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: It is not due to pressure or fear.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I am not afraid of anyone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I cannot be bought by anyone, with money, power, or fame.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I hope to prove this to you and to myself in the coming years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: This life is short, and to me, without integrity, it is not worth living.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: People sometimes talk down to me, call me naive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Perhaps they are right, but it is who I am.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I think this life, this world, this, our human civilization is beautiful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: And, as Dostoevsky said, beauty will save the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: This is the Lex Friedman Podcast, and here's my conversation with Albert Burla.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: The development of the COVID-19 vaccine was one of the greatest accomplishments of science in recent history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: No matter what, this should give people hope for the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: And yet, it is more of a source of division.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I hope we can discuss both the inspiring and the difficult ideas in this conversation, so that we can do our small part in healing this division.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: I hope so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: There were five, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: And in another place, what we call the Data Monitoring Committee, which is a group of experts, independent experts, they are on Pfizer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: we're going to have the opportunity to unblind the data and then tell us if the study needs to continue or if it is successful or if it fails.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: And we were waiting for their call.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: So the call came a little bit later than what we expected, which created a lot of anxiety to all of us, but came around, I think, two o'clock.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: You're just sitting there waiting? What were you feeling?

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Sitting there waiting and teasing one another, drinking coffee, making jokes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Free, liberated, happy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Like if a huge weight that was on my shoulders was lifted.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Listen, maybe it's the Russian thing too. I love love. So I appreciate that kind of celebration.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: So looking back from that moment to before, how much did it cost to develop the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine?

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: You know, we do a lot of that anyway. This is what we do in our daily work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Usually we'll spend 50 millions and then if that goes well, then we will spend another 50.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: And then if it goes well, then 100. Here we put all together a little bit more than $2.3 billion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: we were living at that time. It was a pandemic. People were scared. We were scared. We didn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: know how tomorrow will look like. We were living unprecedented situations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: And we knew that we have capabilities that may help. So there was not a second question or choice.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: We go all in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: When you make decisions like that, you're the CEO of a company that needs to make money

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: world is facing uncertainty and fear and potentially destructive pandemic in the early days just when

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: you're seeing the full uncertainty before us, don't know how it's going to unroll, and how much of it

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: is this may also be a good financial decision to take this risk?

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: Yeah. I think about it all the time and I know very well that if you focus too much on making

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: money, you will never make. You should focus in what is the real value driver. And the real

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: value driver, it is to make breakthroughs that change patients' lives. If you don't do that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: you will never make money. If you do that, don't worry. Things will fall into place and also money

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: sell it or if we don't sell it because what we were focusing 100% was how to bring a solution to the

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: when you do that, you will have good returns as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: of laws that they are forcing regulators and companies to put out their interactions and

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: what exactly was discussed. Now, to go into specific details of some discussions, I don't

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249

body.input: this. There seems to be a bureaucracy that gets in the way of transparency. That's always the

metadata.title: Podcast: Albert Bourla: Pfizer CEO | Lex Fridman Podcast #249
