metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: on top of it, that's a way to democratize it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: That's really interesting, actually.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: And Microsoft throughout its history

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: has been positioned well to do that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: And the, you know, the tie back to this radical markets thing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: like the, so my team has been working with Glenn

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: on this and Jaren Lanier actually.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: So Jaren is the, like the sort of father of virtual reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: Like he's one of the most interesting human beings

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: on the planet, like a sweet, sweet guy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: And so Jaren and Glenn and folks in my team

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: have been working on this notion of data as labor

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: or like they call it data dignity as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: And so the idea is that if you, you know, again,

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: going back to this sort of industrial analogy,

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: if you think about data as the raw material

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: that is consumed by the machine of AI

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: in order to do useful things,

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: then like we're not doing a really great job right now

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: in having transparent marketplaces for valuing

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: those data contributions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: So like, and we all make them like explicitly,

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: like you go to LinkedIn,

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: you sort of set up your profile on LinkedIn.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: Like that's an explicit contribution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: Like, you know exactly the information

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: that you're putting into the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: And like, you put it there because you have

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: some nominal notion of like what value

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: you're gonna get in return.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: But it's like only nominal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: Like you don't know exactly what value

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: you're getting in return.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: Like services free, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: like it's low amount of like perceived debt.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: And then you've got all this indirect contribution

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: that you're making just by virtue of interacting

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: with all of the technology that's in your daily life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: and this data dignity team are trying to do is like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: that let us value those data contributions

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: so that you could create an economy

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: and like a set of controls and incentives

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: that would allow people to like maybe even in the limit,

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: like earn part of their living

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: through the data that they're creating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: And like, you can sort of see it in explicit ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: There are these companies like Scale AI

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: and like there are a whole bunch of them

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: who work for those companies are getting compensated

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: for their data contributions into the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: And so.

body.input: Correct.

body.input: in like how the data is getting used.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: It's true even for these like folks who are getting

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: that performs well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: And so, I think that's one of the challenges.

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

metadata.title: Podcast: Kevin Scott: Microsoft CTO | Lex Fridman Podcast #30

body.input: like through these combinations,

body.input: like how the value is flowing.

body.input: Yeah, that's fascinating.

body.input: Tough.

body.input: that happened long ago, especially in terms of our fear of new things, repeats itself in the modern

body.input: day, and so has many lessons for us to think about in terms of human psychology and the role of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: technology in our society. Anyway, you should subscribe and listen to Pessimists Archive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I highly recommend it. And now here's my conversation with Michael Kearns. You mentioned

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: reading Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas in high school and having a more or a bit more of a

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: literary mind. So what books, non-technical, non-computer science, would you say had the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: biggest impact on your life, either intellectually or emotionally? You've dug deep into my history,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I see. Yeah, I think my favorite novel is Infinite Jest by David Foster Wallace, which

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: actually coincidentally much of it takes place in the halls of buildings right around us here at MIT.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So that certainly had a big influence on me. And as you noticed, when I was in high school,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I actually even started college as an English major. So I was very influenced by that genre

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of journalism at the time and thought I wanted to be a writer and then realized that an English

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: major teaches you to read, but it doesn't teach you how to write. And then I became interested in

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: math and computer science instead. Well, in your new book, Ethical Algorithm, you kind of sneak up

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: from an algorithmic perspective on these deep, profound philosophical questions of fairness,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of privacy. In thinking about these topics, how often do you return to that literary mind

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that you had? Yeah, I'd like to claim there was a deeper connection. But I think both Aaron and I

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: came at these topics first and foremost from a technical angle. I consider myself primarily

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and originally a machine learning researcher. And I think as we just watched the rest of the society,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the field technically advance, and then quickly on the heels of that, the buzzkill of all of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: anti-social behavior by algorithms, just kind of realized there was an opportunity for us to do

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: something about it from a research perspective. More to the point in your question, I do have an

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: uncle who is literally a moral philosopher. And so in the early days of our technical work on

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: fairness topics, I would occasionally run ideas behind him. So I remember an early email I sent

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to him in which I said, oh, here's a specific definition of algorithmic fairness that we think

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is some sort of variant of Rawlsian fairness. What do you think? And I thought I was asking a yes or

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: no question. And I got back to a kind of classical philosopher's response saying, well, it depends.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: If you look at it this way, then you might conclude this. And that's when I realized that there was a

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: real kind of rift between the ways philosophers and others had thought about things like fairness

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: from sort of a humanitarian perspective and the way that you needed to think about it as a computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: scientist if you were going to kind of implement actual algorithmic solutions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: But I would say the algorithmic solutions take care of some of the low-hanging fruit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Sort of the problem is a lot of algorithms, when they don't consider fairness,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: they are just terribly unfair. And when they don't consider privacy, they're terribly,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: they violate privacy. Sort of the algorithmic approach fixes big problems. But there is still,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you get, when you start pushing into the gray area, that's when you start getting into this

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: philosophy of what it means to be fair, starting from Plato. What is justice kind of questions?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Yeah, I think that's right. And I mean, I would even not go as far as you went to say that sort

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of the algorithmic work in these areas is solving the biggest problems. And we discussed in the book

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the fact that really we are, there's a sense in which we're kind of looking where the light is in

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that, for example, if police are racist in who they decide to stop and frisk, and that goes into

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the data, there's sort of no undoing that downstream by kind of clever algorithmic methods.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And I think especially in fairness, I mean, I think less so in privacy, where we feel like

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the community kind of really has settled on the right definition, which is differential privacy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: If you just look at the algorithmic fairness literature already, you can see it's going to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: much more of a mess. And you've got these theorems saying, here are three entirely reasonable

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: desirable notions of fairness, and here's a proof that you cannot simultaneously have all three of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: them. So I think we know that algorithmic fairness compared to algorithmic privacy is going to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: kind of a harder problem. And it will have to revisit, I think, things that have been thought

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: about by many generations of scholars before us. So it's very early days for fairness, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So before we get into the details of differential privacy and on the fairness side,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: let me linger on the philosophy a bit. Do you think most people are fundamentally good,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: or do most of us have both the capacity for good and evil within us?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I mean, I'm an optimist. I tend to think that most people are good and want to do right,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and that deviations from that are usually due to circumstance, not due to people being bad at heart.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: With people with power, are people at the heads of governments, people at the heads of companies,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: people at the heads of maybe, so financial power markets, do you think the distribution there is

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: also, most people are good and have good intent? Yeah, I guess I think that's the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: question. Yeah, I do. I mean, my statement wasn't qualified to people not in positions of power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I mean, I think what happens in a lot of the cliché about absolute power corrupts absolutely. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I think even short of that, having spent a lot of time on Wall Street and also in arenas very,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: very different from Wall Street, like academia, one of the things I think I've benefited from by

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: moving between two very different worlds is you become aware that these worlds kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: develop their own social norms and they develop their own rationales for behavior, for instance,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that might look unusual to outsiders, but when you're in that world, it doesn't feel unusual at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I think this is true of a lot of professional cultures, for instance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And so then you're, maybe slippery slope is too strong of a word, but you're in some world where

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you're mainly around other people with the same kind of viewpoints and training and worldview as

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you. And I think that's more of a source of abuses of power than sort of, they're being good people

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and evil people and that somehow the evil people are the ones that somehow rise to power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Oh, that's really interesting. So it's the within the social norms constructed by that particular

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: group of people, you're all trying to do good, but because it's a group, you might drift into

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: something that for the broader population, it does not align with the values of society. That's the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: word. Yeah. I mean, or not that you drift, but even that things that don't make sense to the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: outside world don't seem unusual to you. So it's not sort of like a good or a bad thing, but,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: like, so for instance, in the world of finance, there's a lot of complicated types of activity

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that if you are not immersed in that world, you cannot see why the purpose of that activity

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: exists at all. It just seems like completely useless and people just pushing money around.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And when you're in that world, and you learn more, your view does become more nuanced.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: You realize, okay, there is actually a function to this activity. And in some cases, you would

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: conclude that actually, if magically we could eradicate this activity tomorrow, it would come

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: back because it actually is serving some useful purpose. It's just a useful purpose that's very

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: difficult for outsiders to see. And so I think lots of professional work environments or cultures,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: as I might put it, kind of have these social norms that don't make sense to the outside world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Academia is the same, right? I mean, lots of people look at academia and say, what the hell

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: are all of you people doing? Why are you paid so much? In some cases, at taxpayer expenses to do...

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Publish papers that nobody reads. But when you're in that world, you come to see the value for it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: but even though you might not be able to explain it to the person in the street.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Right. And in the case of the financial sector, tools like credit might not make sense to people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: It's a good example of something that does seem to pop up and be useful, or just the power of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: markets and just in general, capitalism. Yeah. In finance, I think the primary example I would

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: give is leverage, right? So being allowed to borrow, to sort of use 10 times as much money

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: as you've actually borrowed, right? So that's an example of something that before I had any

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: experience in financial markets, I might've looked at and said, well, what is the purpose of that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: That just seems very dangerous. And it is dangerous, and it has proven dangerous. But if the fact of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the matter is that on some particular time scale, you are holding positions that are very unlikely

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to lose your value at risk or variances like one or 5%, then it kind of makes sense that you'd be

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: allowed to use a little bit more than you have, because you have some confidence that you're not

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: going to lose it all in a single day. Now, of course, when that happens, we've seen what happens

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: not too long ago. But the idea that it serves no useful economic purpose under any circumstances

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is definitely not true. We'll return to the other side of the coast, Silicon Valley, and the problems

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: there as we talk about privacy, as we talk about fairness. At the high level, and I'll ask some

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: sort of basic questions with a hope to get at the fundamental nature of reality, but from a very high

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: level, what is an ethical algorithm? So I can say that an algorithm has a running time of using big

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: O notation, n log n. I can say that a machine learning algorithm classifies cat versus dog with

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: 97% accuracy. Do you think there will one day be a way to measure in the same compelling way as the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: big O notation of this algorithm is 97% ethical? First of all, let me riff for a second on your

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: specific n log n example. Because early in the book, when we're just trying to describe algorithms,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: period, we say, okay, what's an example of an algorithm or an algorithmic problem? First of all,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: it's sorting. You have a bunch of index cards with numbers on them and you want to sort them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And we describe an algorithm that sweeps all the way through, finds the smallest number, puts it

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: at the front, then sweeps through again, finds the second smallest number. So we make the point that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: this is an algorithm and it's also a bad algorithm in the sense that it's quadratic rather than n

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: log n, which we know is kind of optimal for sorting. And we make the point that sort of like...

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So even within the confines of a very precisely specified problem, there might be many, many

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: different algorithms for the same problem with different properties. Some might be faster in

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: terms of running time, some might use less memory, some might have better distributed

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: implementations. And so the point is that already we're used to in computer science thinking about

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: trade-offs between different types of quantities and resources and there being better and worse

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: algorithms. And our book is about that part of algorithmic ethics that we know how to kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: put on that same kind of quantitative footing right now. So just to say something that our book is not

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: about, our book is not about kind of broad fuzzy notions of fairness. It's about very specific

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: notions of fairness. There's more than one of them. There are tensions between them, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: But if you pick one of them, you can do something akin to saying that this algorithm is 97% ethical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: You can say, for instance, for this lending model, the false rejection rate on black people and white

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: people is within 3%, right? So we might call that a 97% ethical algorithm and a 100% ethical algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: would mean that that difference is 0%. In that case, fairness is specified when two groups,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: however they're defined, are given to you. That's right. And then you can sort of mathematically

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: start describing the algorithm. But nevertheless, the part where the two groups are given to you,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: unlike running time, we don't in computer science talk about how fast an algorithm feels like when

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: it runs. True. We measure it and ethical starts getting into feelings. So for example, an algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: runs, you know, if it runs in the background, it doesn't disturb the performance of my system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: It'll feel nice. I'll be okay with it. But if it overloads the system, it'll feel unpleasant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So in that same way, ethics, there's a feeling of how socially acceptable it is. How does it represent

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the moral standards of our society today? So in that sense, and sorry to linger on that first

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: high-level philosophical question, do you have a sense we'll be able to measure how ethical an

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: algorithm is? First of all, I certainly didn't mean to give the impression that you can kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: measure memory speed trade-offs and that there's a complete mapping from that onto kind of fairness,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: for instance, or ethics and accuracy, for example. In the type of fairness definitions that are

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: largely the objects of study today and starting to be deployed, you as the user of the definitions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you need to make some hard decisions before you even get to the point of designing fair algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: One of them, for instance, is deciding who it is that you're worried about protecting,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: who you're worried about being harmed by, for instance, some notion of discrimination or

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: unfairness. And then you need to also decide what constitutes harm. So for instance, in a lending

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: application, maybe you decide that falsely rejecting a credit-worthy individual, sort of a false

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: negative, is the real harm and that false positives, i.e. people that are not credit-worthy or are not

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: going to repay your loan, that get a loan, you might think of them as lucky. And so that's not

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: a harm, although it's not clear that if you don't have the means to repay a loan, that being given

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: a loan is not also a harm. So the literature is sort of so far quite limited in that you sort of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: need to say, who do you want to protect and what would constitute harm to that group? And when you

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: ask questions like, will algorithms feel ethical, one way in which they won't, under the definitions

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that I'm describing is if you are an individual who is falsely denied a loan, incorrectly denied

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: a loan, all of these definitions basically say like, well, your compensation is the knowledge

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that we are also falsely denying loans to other people in other groups at the same rate that we're

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: doing it to you. And so there is actually this interesting, even technical tension in the field

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: right now between these sort of group notions of fairness and notions of fairness that might

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: actually feel like real fairness to individuals. They might really feel like their particular

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: interests are being protected or thought about by the algorithm rather than just the groups

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that they happen to be members of. Is there parallels to the big O notation of worst case

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: analysis? So is it important to looking at the worst violation of fairness for an individual,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is it important to minimize that one individual? So like worst case analysis, is that something

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you think about or? I mean, I think we're not even at the point where we can sensibly think

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: about that. So first of all, we're talking here both about fairness applied at the group level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: which is a relatively weak thing, but it's better than nothing. And also the more ambitious thing of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: trying to give some individual promises. But even that doesn't incorporate, I think something that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you're hinting at here is what I might call subjective fairness, right? So a lot of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: definitions, I mean, all of the definitions in the algorithmic fairness literature are what I would

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: kind of call received wisdom definitions. It's sort of, somebody like me sits around and things

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: like, okay, I think here's a technical definition of fairness that I think people should want, or

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that they should think of as some notion of fairness, maybe not the only one, maybe not the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: best one, maybe not the last one. But we really actually don't know from a subjective standpoint,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: like what people really think is fair. We just started doing a little bit of work in our group

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: at actually doing kind of human subject experiments in which we ask people about,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: we ask them questions about fairness, we survey them, we show them pairs of individuals in,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: let's say, a criminal recidivism prediction setting. And we ask them, do you think these

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: two individuals should be treated the same as a matter of fairness? And to my knowledge,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to my knowledge, there's not a large literature in which ordinary people are asked about,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: they have sort of notions of their subjective fairness elicited from them. It's mainly

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: scholars who think about fairness, kind of making up their own definitions. And I think this needs

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to change actually for many social norms, not just for fairness. So there's a lot of discussion

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: these days in the AI community about interpretable AI or understandable AI. And as far as I can tell,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: everybody agrees that deep learning or at least the outputs of deep learning are not very

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: understandable. And people might agree that sparse linear models with integer coefficients are more

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: understandable. But nobody's really asked people. There's very little literature on sort of showing

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: people models and asking them, do they understand what the model is doing? And I think that in all

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: these topics, as these fields mature, we need to start doing more behavioral work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Yeah, which is one of my deep passions is psychology. And I always thought computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: scientists will be the best future psychologists. In a sense, that data is, especially in this

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: modern world, the data is a really powerful way to understand and study human behavior. And you've

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: explored that with your game theory side of work as well. Yeah, I'd like to think that what you say

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is true about computer scientists and psychology from my own limited wandering into human subject

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: experiments, we have a great deal to learn. Not just computer science, but AI and machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: learning more specifically, I kind of think of as imperialist research communities in that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: kind of like physicists in an earlier generation. Computer scientists kind of don't think of any

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: scientific topic as off limits to them. They will freely wander into areas that others have

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: been thinking about for decades or longer. And we usually tend to embarrass ourselves

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in those efforts for some amount of time. I think reinforcement learning is a good example. So a lot

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of the early work in reinforcement learning, I have complete sympathy for the control theorists

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that looked at this and said like, okay, you are reinventing stuff that we've known since like the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: 40s, right? But in my view, eventually, the sort of computer scientists have made significant

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: contributions to that field, even though we kind of embarrassed ourselves for the first decade.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So I think if computer scientists are going to start engaging in kind of psychology, human subjects,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: type of research, we should expect to be embarrassing ourselves for a good 10 years or so,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and then hope that it turns out as well as some other areas that we've waded into.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So you kind of mentioned this, just to linger on the idea of an ethical algorithm,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: an idea of groups, sort of group thinking and individual thinking. And we're struggling that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And one of the amazing things about algorithms and your book and just this field of study is

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: it gets us to ask, like forcing machines, converting these ideas into algorithms is forcing

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: us to ask questions of ourselves as a human civilization. So there's a lot of people now

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in public discourse doing sort of group thinking, thinking like there's particular sets of groups

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that we don't want to discriminate against and so on. And then there is individuals,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: sort of in the individual life stories, the struggles they went through and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Now, like in philosophy, it's easier to do group thinking because you don't,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you know, it's very hard to think about individuals. There's so much variability. But with data,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you can start to actually say, you know, what group thinking is too crude. You're actually

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: doing more discrimination by thinking in terms of groups and individuals. Can you linger on

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that kind of idea of group versus individual and ethics? And is it good to continue thinking in

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: terms of groups in algorithms? So let me start by answering a very good high-level question with a

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: slightly narrow technical response, which is these group definitions of fairness, like here's a few

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: groups, like different racial groups, maybe gender groups, maybe age, what have you. And let's make

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: sure that, you know, for none of these groups, do we, you know, have a false negative rate,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: which is much higher than any other one of these groups. Okay. So these are kind of classic group

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: aggregate notions of fairness. And, you know, but at the end of the day, an individual you can think

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of as a combination of all of their attributes, right? They're a member of a racial group. They

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: have a gender. They have an age, you know, and many other, you know, demographic properties that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: are not biological, but that, you know, are still, you know, very strong determinants of outcome and

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: personality and the like. So one, I think, useful spectrum is to sort of think about that array

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: between the group and the specific individual and to realize that in some ways, asking for fairness

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: at the individual level is to sort of ask for group fairness simultaneously for all possible

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: combinations of groups. So in particular, so in particular, you know, if I build a predictive

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: model that meets some definition of fairness by race, by gender, by age, by what have you,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: marginally, to get it slightly technical, sort of independently, I shouldn't expect that model to

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: not discriminate against disabled Hispanic women over age 55, making less than $50,000 a year

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: annually, even though I might have protected each one of those attributes marginally.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So the optimization, actually, that's a fascinating way to put it. So you're just optimizing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the one way to achieve the optimizing fairness for individuals, just to add more and more

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: definitions of groups that each individual belongs to.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So, you know, at the end of the day, we could think of all of ourselves as groups of size one,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: because eventually there's some attribute that separates you from me and everybody from

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: everybody else in the world. Okay. And so it is possible to put, you know, these incredibly

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: coarse ways of thinking about fairness and these very, very individualistic specific ways

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: on a common scale. And, you know, one of the things we've worked on from a research perspective is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you know, so we sort of know how to, you know, in relative terms, we know how to provide fairness

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: guarantees at the coarsest end of the scale. We don't know how to provide kind of sensible,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: tractable, realistic fairness guarantees at the individual level, but maybe we could start

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: creeping towards that by dealing with more, you know, refined subgroups. I mean, we gave a name

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to this phenomenon where, you know, you protect, you enforce some definition of fairness

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: for a bunch of marginal attributes or features, but then you find yourself discriminating against

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: a combination of them. We call that fairness gerrymandering, because like political

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: gerrymandering, you know, you're giving some guarantee at the aggregate level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: but that when you kind of look in a more granular way at what's going on, you realize that you're

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: achieving that aggregate guarantee by sort of favoring some groups and discriminating against

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: other ones. And so there are, you know, it's early days, but there are algorithmic approaches

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that let you start creeping towards that, you know, individual end of the spectrum.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Does there need to be human input in the form of weighing the value of the importance of each kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of group? So for example, is it like, so gender, say, crudely speaking, male and female, and then

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: different races, are we as humans supposed to put value on saying gender is 0.6 and race is 0.4

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in terms of, in the big optimization of achieving fairness? Is that kind of what humans...

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I mean, of course, you know, I don't need to tell you that, of course, technically one could

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: incorporate such weights if you wanted to into a definition of fairness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: You know, fairness is an interesting topic in that having worked in the book being about

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: both fairness, privacy, and many other social norms. Fairness, of course, is a much, much more

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: loaded topic. So privacy, I mean, people want privacy, people don't like violations of privacy,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: violations of privacy cause damage, angst, and bad publicity for the companies that are victims of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: But sort of everybody agrees, more data privacy would be better than less data privacy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And you don't have these, somehow the discussions of fairness don't become politicized along other

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: dimensions like race and about gender and whether we... And you quickly find yourself

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: kind of revisiting topics that have been kind of unresolved forever, like affirmative action,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: right? Sort of like, why are you protecting... Some people will say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: why are you protecting this particular racial group? And others will say, well, we need to do that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: as a matter of retribution. Other people will say it's a matter of economic opportunity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And I don't know which of... Whether any of these are the right answers, but you sort of... Fairness

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is sort of special in that as soon as you start talking about it, you inevitably have to participate

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in debates about fair to whom, at what expense to who else. I mean, even in criminal justice,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: right? Where people talk about fairness in criminal sentencing or predicting failures to appear or

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: making parole decisions or the like, they'll point out that, well, these definitions of fairness are

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: all about fairness for the criminals and what about fairness for the victims, right? So when I

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: basically say something like, well, the false incarceration rate for black people and white

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: people needs to be roughly the same, there's no mention of potential victims of criminals in such

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: a fairness definition. And that's the realm of public discourse. I should actually recommend...

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I just listened to people listening, Intelligence Squares Debates, US Edition just had a debate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: They have this structure where you have old Oxford style or whatever they're called, debates,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and it was two versus two and they talked about affirmative action. And it was incredibly

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: interesting that it's still... There's really good points on every side of this issue, which is

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: fascinating to listen to. Yeah, yeah, I agree. And so it's interesting to be a researcher trying to do,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: for the most part, technical algorithmic work, but Aaron and I both quickly learned you cannot

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: do that and then go out and talk about it and expect people to take it seriously if you're

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: unwilling to engage in these broader debates that are entirely extra algorithmic, right? They're

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: not about algorithms and making algorithms better. They're sort of, as you said, sort of like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: what should society be protecting in the first place? When you discuss the fairness, an algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that achieves fairness, whether in the constraints and the objective function,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: there's an immediate kind of analysis you can perform, which is saying, if you care about

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: fairness in gender, this is the amount that you have to pay for in terms of the performance of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the system. Is there a role for statements like that in a table in a paper or do you want to

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: really not touch that? No, we want to touch that and we do touch it. So, I mean, just again,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to make sure I'm not promising your viewers more than we know how to provide. But if you pick a

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: definition of fairness, like I'm worried about gender discrimination, and you pick a notion of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: harm, like false rejection for a loan, for example, and you give me a model, I can definitely, first

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of all, go audit that model. It's easy for me to go from data to kind of say like, okay, your false

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: rejection rate on women is this much higher than it is on men. But once you also put the fairness

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: into your objective function, I mean, I think the table that you're talking about is what we would

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: call the Pareto curve, right? You can literally trace out, and we give examples of such plots on

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: real data sets in the book. You have two axes. On the X axis is your error. On the Y axis is

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: unfairness by whatever, if it's like the disparity between false rejection rates between two groups.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And your algorithm now has a knob that basically says, how strongly do I want to enforce fairness?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And the less unfair, if the two axes are error and unfairness, we'd like to be at zero zero.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: We'd like zero error and zero unfair unfairness simultaneously. Anybody who works in machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: learning knows that you're generally not going to get to zero error, period, without any fairness

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: constraint whatsoever. So that's not gonna happen. But in general, you'll get some kind of convex

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: curve that specifies the numerical trade-off you face. If I wanna go from 17% error down to

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: 16% error, what will be the increase in unfairness that I've experienced as a result of that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And so this curve specifies the kind of undominated models. Models that are off that curve

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: can be strictly improved in one or both dimensions. You can either make the error better or the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: unfairness better or both. And I think our view is that not only are these two curves

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: are these objects, these Pareto curves, efficient frontiers as you might call them,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: not only are they valuable scientific objects, I actually think that they in the near term

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: might need to be the interface between researchers working in the field and stakeholders in given

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: problems. So you could really imagine telling a criminal jurisdiction, look, if you're concerned

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: about racial fairness, but you're also concerned about accuracy, you want to release on parole

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: people that are not going to recommit a violent crime and you don't wanna release the ones who are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So that's accuracy. But if you also care about the mistakes you make not being disproportionately

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: on one racial group or another, you can show this curve. I'm hoping that in the near future,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: it'll be possible to explain these curves to non-technical people that are the ones that have

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to make the decision, where do we wanna be on this curve? What are the relative merits or value of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: having lower error versus lower unfairness? That's not something computer scientists should be

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: deciding for society. The people in the field, so to speak, the policy makers, the regulators,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that's who should be making these decisions. But I think and hope that they can be made to understand

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that these trade-offs generally exist and that you need to pick a point and ignoring the trade-off,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you're implicitly picking a point anyway. You just don't know it and you're not admitting it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Just to linger on the point of trade-offs, I think that's a really important thing to think about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: You think when we start to optimize for fairness, there's almost always in most systems going to be

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: trade-offs. What's the trade-off between, just to clarify, there have been some technical terms

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: thrown around, but a perfectly fair world. Why will somebody be upset about that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: The specific trade-off I talked about just in order to make things very concrete was between

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: numerical error and some numerical measure of unfairness.
