metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: What is numerical error in the case of- Just say predictive error, the probability or

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: frequency with which you release somebody on parole who then goes on to recommit a violent crime or

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: keep incarcerated somebody who would not have recommitted a violent crime.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: In the case of awarding somebody parole or giving somebody parole or letting them out on parole,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you don't want them to recommit a crime. Your system failed in prediction if they happen to do a

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: crime. Okay, so that's one axis. What's the fairness axis?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And so then the fairness axis might be the difference between racial groups in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: false positive predictions, namely people that I kept incarcerated

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: predicting that they would recommit a violent crime when in fact they wouldn't have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Right. And the unfairness of that, just to linger it and allow me to

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: ineliquently to try to sort of describe why that's unfair, why unfairness is there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: The unfairness you want to get rid of is that in the judge's mind, the bias of having been

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: brought up to society, the slight racial bias, the racism that exists in the society,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you want to remove that from the system. Another way that's been debated is sort of equality

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of opportunity versus equality of outcome. And there's a weird dance there that's really

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: difficult to get right. And we don't, it's affirmative action is exploring that space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Right. And then we, this also quickly bleeds into questions like, well,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: maybe if one group really does recommit crimes at a higher rate, the reason for that is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: at some earlier point in the pipeline or earlier in their lives, they didn't receive the same

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: resources that the other group did. And so there's always in kind of fairness discussions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the possibility that the real injustice came earlier, earlier in this individual's life,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: earlier in this group's history, et cetera, et cetera. And so a lot of the fairness discussion

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is almost, the goal is for it to be a corrective mechanism to account for the injustice earlier

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in life. By some definitions of fairness or some theories of fairness, yeah. Others would say like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: look, it's not to correct that injustice, it's just to kind of level the playing field right now and

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: not falsely incarcerate more people of one group than another group. But I mean, I think it might

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: be helpful just to demystify a little bit about the many ways in which bias or unfairness can come

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: into algorithms, especially in the machine learning era, right? And I think many of your

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: viewers have probably heard these examples before, but let's say I'm building a face recognition

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: system, right? And so I'm kind of gathering lots of images of faces and trying to train the system

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to recognize new faces of those individuals from training on a training set of those faces of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: individuals. And it shouldn't surprise anybody or certainly not anybody in the field of machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: learning if my training data set was primarily white males and I'm, I'm not a white male,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I'm training that, the model to maximize the overall accuracy on my training data set that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the model can reduce its error most by getting things right on the white males that constitute

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the majority of the data set, even if that means that on other groups, they will be less accurate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Now there's a bunch of ways you could think about addressing this. One is to deliberately

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: put into the objective of the algorithm not to, not to optimize the error at the expense of this

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: discrimination. And then you're kind of back in the land of these kind of two-dimensional numerical

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: trade-offs. A valid counter argument is to say like, well, no, you don't have to, there's no,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you know, the, the, the notion of the tension between error and accuracy here is a false one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Mm-hmm. You could instead just go out and get much more data on these other groups that are in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: minority and, you know, equalize your data set, or you could train a separate model on those subgroups

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and, you know, have multiple models. The point I think we would, you know, we've tried to make in

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the book is that those things have cost too, right? Right. Going out and gathering more data

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: on groups that are relatively rare compared to your plurality or majority group that, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: it may not cost you in the accuracy of the model, but it's going to cost, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: it's going to cost the company developing this model more money to develop that. And it also

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: costs more money to build separate predictive models and to implement and deploy them. So even

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: if you can find a way to avoid the tension between error and accuracy in training a model,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you might push the cost somewhere else, like money, like development time, research time, and the like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: There are fundamentally difficult philosophical questions in fairness,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and we live in a very divisive political climate, outrage culture. There is alt-right folks on 4chan,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: trolls. There is social justice warriors on Twitter. There is very divisive, outraged folks

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: on all sides of every kind of system. How do you, how do we as engineers build ethical algorithms

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in such divisive culture? Do you think they could be disjoint? The human has to inject your values

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and then you can optimize over those values. But in our times when you start actually applying

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: these systems, things get a little bit challenging for the public discourse. How do you think we can

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: proceed? Yeah, I mean, for the most part in the book, you know, a point that we try to take some

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: pains to make is that we don't view ourselves or people like us as being in the position of deciding

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: for society what the right social norms are, what the right definitions of fairness are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Our main point is to just show that if society or the relevant stakeholders in a particular domain

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: can come to agreement on those sorts of things, there's a way of encoding that into algorithms in

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: many cases, not in all cases. One other misconception that hopefully we definitely dispel is sometimes

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: people read the title of the book and I think not unnaturally fear that what we're suggesting is

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that the algorithms themselves should decide what those social norms are and develop their own

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: notions of fairness and privacy or ethics. And we're definitely not suggesting that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: The title of the book is ethical algorithm, by the way, and I didn't think of that interpretation

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of the title. That's interesting. Yeah, yeah. I mean, especially these days where people are

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: concerned about the robots becoming our overlords, the idea that the robots will be our overlords,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: robots would also develop their own social norms is just one step away from that. But I do think,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: obviously, despite disclaimer that people like us shouldn't be making those decisions for society,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: we are living in a world where in many ways computer scientists have made some decisions

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that have fundamentally changed the nature of our society and democracy and civil discourse and

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: deliberation in ways that I think most people generally feel are bad these days. Right? So.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: But they had to make, so if we look at people at the heads of companies and so on,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: they had to make those decisions, right? There has to be decisions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So there's two options. Either you kind of put your head in the sand and don't think about these

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: things and just let the algorithm do what it does, or you make decisions about what you value

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: over injecting moral values into the algorithm. Look, I never mean to be an apologist for the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: tech industry, but I think it's a little bit too far to sort of say that explicit decisions

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: were made about these things. So let's, for instance, take social media platforms, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So like many inventions in technology and computer science, a lot of these platforms

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that we now use regularly kind of started as curiosities, right? I remember when things

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: like Facebook came out and its predecessors like Friendster, which nobody even remembers now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: people really wonder like why would anybody want to spend time doing that? Even the web,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: when it first came out, when it wasn't populated with much content and it was largely kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: hobbyists building their own kind of ramshackle websites, a lot of people looked at this and

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: said, well, what is the purpose of this thing? Why is this interesting? Who would want to do this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So even things like Facebook and Twitter, yes, technical decisions were made by engineers,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: by scientists, by executives in the design of those platforms. But I don't think

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: 10 years ago anyone anticipated that those platforms, for instance, might kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: acquire undue influence on political discourse or on the outcomes of elections,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and I think the scrutiny that these companies are getting now is entirely appropriate, but I think

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: it's a little too harsh to kind of look at history and sort of say like, oh, you should have been

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: able to anticipate that this would happen with your platform. And in the sort of gaming chapter

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of the book, one of the points we're making is that these platforms, right, they don't operate

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in isolation. So unlike the other topics we're discussing like fairness and privacy, like those

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: are really cases where algorithms can operate on your data and make decisions about you, and you're

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: not even aware of it, okay? Things like Facebook and Twitter, these are systems, right? These are

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: social systems, and their evolution, even their technical evolution, because machine learning is

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: involved, is driven in no small part by the behavior of the users themselves and how the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: users decide to adopt them and how to use them. And so, you know, I think that's a really

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: interesting point. And so, you know, I'm kind of like, who really knew that, you know, until

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: we saw it happen, who knew that these things might be able to influence the outcome of elections?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Who knew that, you know, they might polarize political discourse because of the ability to,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you know, decide who you interact with on the platform and also with the platform

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: naturally using machine learning to optimize for your own interests that they would further

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: isolate us from each other and, you know, like feed us all basically just the stuff that we

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: already agreed with. And so, I think, you know, we've come to that outcome, I think, largely,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: but I think it's something that we all learned together, including the companies, as these

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: things happen. Now, you asked like, well, are there algorithmic remedies to these kinds of things? And

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: again, these are big problems that are not going to be solved with, you know, somebody going in

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and changing a few lines of code somewhere in a social media platform. But I do think in many

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: ways, there are definitely ways of making things better. I mean, like an obvious recommendation

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that we make at some point in the book is like, look, you know, to the extent that we think that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: machine learning applied for personalization purposes in things like newsfeed, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: or other platforms has led to polarization and intolerance of opposing viewpoints.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: As you know, right, these algorithms have models, right, and they kind of place people in some kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of metric space and they place content in that space and they sort of know the extent to which

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I have an affinity for a particular type of content. And by the same token, they also probably have,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that same model probably gives you a good idea of the stuff I'm likely to violently disagree with or

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: be offended by. Okay. So, you know, in this case, there really is some knob you could tune that says

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: like, instead of showing people only what they like and what they want, let's show them some stuff

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that we think that they don't like, or that's a little bit further away. And you could even

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: imagine users being able to control this, you know, just like everybody gets a slider and that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: slider says like, you know, how much stuff do you want to see that's kind of, you know, you might

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: disagree with, or is at least further from your interests. It's almost like an exploration button.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So just get your intuition. Do you think engagement, so like you're staying on the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: platform, you're staying engaged. Do you think fairness, ideas of fairness won't emerge? Like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: how bad is it to just optimize for engagement? Do you think we'll run into big trouble if we're just

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: optimizing for how much you love the platform? Well, I mean, optimizing for engagement kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: got us where we are. So do you one, have faith that it's possible to do better? And two, if it is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: how do we do better? I mean, it's definitely possible to do different, right? And again,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you know, it's not as if I think that doing something different than optimizing for engagement

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: won't cost these companies in real ways, including revenue and profitability potentially.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: In the short term, at least. Yeah, in the short term, right. And again, you know, if I worked at

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: these companies, I'm sure that it would have seemed like the most natural thing in the world also to

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: want to optimize engagement, right? And that's good for users in some sense. You want them to be,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you know, vested in the platform and enjoying it and finding it useful, interesting, and or productive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: But, you know, my point is, is that the idea that there's, that it's sort of out of their hands,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: as you said, or that there's nothing to do about it, never say never, but that strikes me as

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: implausible as a machine learning person, right? I mean, these companies are driven by machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: learning and this optimization of engagement is essentially driven by machine learning, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: It's driven by not just machine learning, but, you know, very, very large scale A, B experimentation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: where you kind of tweak some element of the user interface or tweak some component of an algorithm

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: or tweak some component or feature of your click through prediction model. And my point is, is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: anytime you know how to optimize for something, you, you know, by def, almost by definition,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that solution tells you how not to optimize for it or to do something different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Engagement can be measured. So sort of optimizing for sort of minimizing divisiveness or maximizing

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: intellectual growth over the lifetime of a human being are very difficult to measure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: That, that's right. So I'm not, I'm not claiming that doing something different will

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: immediately make it apparent that this is a good thing for society. And in particular, I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I think one way of thinking about where we are on some of these social media platforms is that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you know, it kind of feels a bit like we're in a bad equilibrium, right? That these systems are

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: helping us all kind of optimize something myopically and selfishly for ourselves. And of course,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: from an individual standpoint at any given moment, like why would I want to see things in my newsfeed

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that I found irrelevant, offensive or, you know, or the like, okay. But, you know, maybe by all of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: us, you know, having these platforms myopically optimized in our interests, we have reached a

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: collective outcome as a society that we're unhappy with in different ways. Let's say with respect to

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: things like, you know, political discourse and tolerance of opposing viewpoints. And if Mark

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Zuckerberg gave you a call and said, I'm thinking of taking a sabbatical, could you run Facebook for

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: me for six months? What would you, how? I think no thanks would be my first response, but

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: there are many aspects of being the head of the entire company that are kind of entirely

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: exogenous to many of the things that we're discussing here. And so I don't really think

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I would need to be CEO of Facebook to kind of implement the, you know, more limited set of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: solutions that I might imagine. But I think one concrete thing they could do is they could

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: experiment with letting people who chose to, to see more stuff in their newsfeed that is not entirely

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: kind of chosen to optimize for their particular interests, beliefs, et cetera. So the, the kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of thing is, so I could speak to YouTube, but I think Facebook probably does something similar

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is they're quite effective at automatically finding what sorts of groups you belong to,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: not based on race or gender or so on, but based on the kind of stuff you enjoy watching.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And the case of YouTube sort of, it's a difficult thing for Facebook or YouTube to then say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: well, you know what, we're going to show you something from a very different cluster.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Even though we believe algorithmically, you're unlikely to enjoy that thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Sort of, that's a weird jump to make. There has to be a human, like at the very top of that system

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that says, well, that will be long-term healthy for you. That's more than an algorithmic decision.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Or that same person could say that'll be long-term healthy for the platform.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: The platform.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Or for the platform's influence on society outside of the platform.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And it's easy for me to sit here and say these things, but conceptually, I do not think that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: these are kind of totally, or they shouldn't be kind of completely alien ideas. You could try

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: things like this, and it wouldn't be, we wouldn't have to invent entirely new science to do it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: because if we're all already embedded in some metric space and there's a notion of distance

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: between you and me and every piece of content, then we know exactly, the same model that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: dictates how to make me really happy also tells how to make me as unhappy as possible as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Right. The focus in your book and algorithmic fairness research today in general is on machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: learning, like we said, is data. And just even the entire AI field right now is captivated with

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: machine learning, with deep learning. Do you think ideas in symbolic AI or totally other kinds of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: approaches are interesting, useful in this space, have some promising ideas in terms of fairness?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I haven't thought about that question specifically in the context of fairness. I definitely would

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: agree with that statement in the large, right? I mean, I am one of many machine learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: researchers who do believe that the great successes that have been shown in machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: learning recently are great successes, but they're on a pretty narrow set of tasks. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I don't think we're notably closer to general artificial intelligence now than we were when

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I started my career. I mean, there's been progress. And I do think that we are, as a community,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: maybe looking a bit where the light is, but the light is shining pretty bright there right now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and we're finding a lot of stuff. So I don't want to argue with the progress that's been made

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in areas like deep learning, for example. This touches another sort of related thing

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that you mentioned and that people might misinterpret from the title of your book,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: ethical algorithm. Is it possible for the algorithm to automate some of those decisions?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Sort of higher level decisions of what kind of... Like what should be fair?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: What should be fair? The more you know about a field, the more aware you are of its limitations.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And so I'm pretty leery of sort of trying... There's so much we don't all... We already

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: don't know in fairness, even when we're the ones picking the fairness definitions and comparing

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: alternatives and thinking about the tensions between different definitions, that the idea of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: kind of letting the algorithm start exploring as well, I definitely think... This is a much

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: narrower statement. I definitely think that kind of algorithmic auditing for different types of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: unfairness, right? So like in this gerrymandering example, where I might want to prevent not just

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: discrimination against very broad categories, but against combinations of broad categories.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: You quickly get to a point where there's a lot of categories, there's a lot of combinations

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of end features, and you can use algorithmic techniques to sort of try to find the subgroups

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: on which you're discriminating the most and try to fix that. That's actually kind of the form of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the form of one of the algorithms we developed for this fairness gerrymandering problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: But I'm... Partly because of our scientific ignorance on these topics right now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and also partly just because these topics are so loaded emotionally for people,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that I just don't see the value... I mean, again, never say never, but I just don't think we're at

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: a moment where it's a great time for computer scientists to be rolling out the idea like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: hey, not only have we kind of figured fairness out, but we think the algorithm should start

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: deciding what's fair or giving input on that decision. I just don't... The cost benefit

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: analysis to the field of kind of going there right now just doesn't seem worth it to me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: 05.00 That said, I should say that I think computer scientists should be more philosophically...

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Should enrich their thinking about these kinds of things. I think it's been too often used as an

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: excuse for roboticists working on autonomous vehicles, for example, to not think about the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: human factor or psychology or safety. In the same way, computer scientists and algorithms

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that have been sort of using it as an excuse. And I think it's time for basically everybody

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to become computer scientists. 06.00 I was about to agree with everything

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you said except that last point. I think that the other way of looking at it is that I think

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: computer scientists, and many of us are, but we need to wade out into the world more. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: just the influence that computer science and therefore computer scientists have had on society

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: at large just has exponentially magnified in the last 10 or 20 years or so. And before when we were

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: just tinkering around amongst ourselves and it didn't matter that much, there was no need for

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: sort of computer scientists to be citizens of the world more broadly. And I think those days need

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to be over very, very fast. And I'm not saying everybody needs to do it, but to me, the right

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: way of doing it is to not to sort of think that everybody else is going to become a computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: scientist. But I think people are becoming more sophisticated about computer science, even lay

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: people. I think one of the reasons we decided to write this book is we thought 10 years ago,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I wouldn't have tried this just because I just didn't think that sort of people's awareness of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: algorithms and machine learning, the general population would have been high. And you would

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: have had to first write one of the many books kind of just explicating that topic to a lay audience

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: first. Now I think we're at the point where lots of people without any technical training at all

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: know enough about algorithms and machine learning that you can start getting to these nuances of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: things like ethical algorithms. I think we agree that there needs to be much more mixing, but I

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: think a lot of the onus of that mixing needs to be on the computer science community.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Yeah, so just to linger on the disagreement, because I do disagree with you on the point that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I think if you're a biologist, if you're a chemist, if you're an MBA business person,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: all of those things you can, like if you learn to program, and not only program, if you learn to do

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: machine learning, if you learn to do data science, you immediately become much more powerful in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: kinds of things you can do. And therefore, literature, like library sciences, like so

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you were speaking, I think, I think it holds true what you're saying for the next few years, but

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: long term, if you're interested, to me, if you're interested in philosophy, you should learn to

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: program, because then you can scrape data and study what people are thinking about on Twitter,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and then start making philosophical conclusions about the meaning of life. I just feel like

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the access to data, the digitization of whatever problem you're trying to solve, it fundamentally

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: changes what it means to be a computer scientist. I mean, computer scientists in 20, 30 years will

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: go back to being Donald Knuth style theoretical computer science, and everybody would be doing

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: basically, they kind of exploring the kinds of ideas that you're exploring in your book.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: It won't be a computer science major.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Yeah, I mean, I don't think I disagree enough, but I think that that trend of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: more and more people and more and more disciplines adopting ideas from computer science,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: learning how to code, I think that that trend seems firmly underway. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: like an interesting digressive question along these lines is maybe in 50 years,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: there won't be computer science departments anymore, because the field will just sort of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: be ambient in all of the different disciplines. And people will look back and having a computer

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: science department will look like having an electricity department or something. It's like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: everybody uses this, it's just out there. I mean, I do think there will always be that kind of Knuth

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: style core to it, but it's not an implausible path that we kind of get to the point where

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the academic discipline of computer science becomes somewhat marginalized

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: because of its very success in kind of infiltrating all of science and society and the humanities,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: et cetera. What is differential privacy or more broadly algorithmic privacy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Algorithmic privacy more broadly is just the study or the notion of privacy definitions

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: or norms being encoded inside of algorithms. And so, I think we count among this body of work,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: just the literature and practice of things like data anonymization, which we kind of at the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: beginning of our discussion of privacy say like, okay, this is sort of a notion of algorithmic

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: privacy. It kind of tells you something to go do with data. But our view is that it's, and I think

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: this is now quite widespread, that it's, despite the fact that those notions of anonymization

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: kind of redacting and coarsening are the most widely adopted technical solutions for data

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: privacy, they are like deeply fundamentally flawed. And so, to your first question, what is

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: differential privacy? Differential privacy seems to be a much, much better notion of privacy

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that kind of avoids a lot of the weaknesses of anonymization notions while still letting us do

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: useful stuff with data. What's anonymization of data?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So, by anonymization, I'm kind of referring to techniques like I have a database. The rows of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that database are let's say individual people's medical records. And I want to let people use

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that data. Maybe I want to let researchers access that data to build predictive models for some

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: disease. But I'm worried that that will leak sensitive information about specific people's

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: medical records. So, anonymization broadly refers to the set of techniques where I say like, okay,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I'm first going to delete the column with people's names. I'm going to not put, so that would be like

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: a redaction, right? I'm just redacting that information. I am going to take ages, and I'm

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: not going to say your exact age. I'm going to say whether you're zero to 10, 10 to 20, 20 to 30.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I might put the first three digits of your zip code, but not the last two, et cetera, et cetera.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And so, the idea is that through some series of operations like this on the data, I anonymize it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Another term of art that's used is removing personally identifiable information. And this

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is basically the most common way of providing data privacy, but that it's in a way that still lets

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: people access some variant form of the data. So, at a slightly broader

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: picture as you talk about what does anonymization mean when you have multiple

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: databases like with a Netflix prize when you can start combining stuff together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So, this is exactly the problem with these notions, right? Is that notions of anonymization,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: removing personally identifiable information, the kind of fundamental conceptual flaw is that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: these definitions kind of pretend as if the data set in question is the only data set that exists

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in the world or that ever will exist in the future. And of course, things like the Netflix

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: prize and many, many other examples since the Netflix prize, I think that was one of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: earliest ones though. You can re-identify people that were anonymized in the data set by taking

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that anonymized data set and combining it with other allegedly anonymized data sets and maybe

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: publicly available information about you. For people who don't know, the Netflix prize

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: was being publicly released as data. So, the names from those rows were removed, but what was released

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is the preference or the ratings of what movies you like and you don't like. And from that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: combined with other things, I think foreign posts and so on, you can start to figure out the names.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: That case, it was specifically the internet movie database where lots of Netflix users publicly rate

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: their movie preferences. And so, the anonymized data in Netflix, it's just this phenomenon,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: I think, that we've all come to realize in the last decade or so is that just knowing a few

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: apparently irrelevant, innocuous things about you can often act as a fingerprint. If I know

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: what rating you gave to these 10 movies and the date on which you entered these movies,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: this is almost like a fingerprint for you in the sea of all Netflix users. There was just another

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: paper on this in Science or Nature about a month ago that 18 attributes. My favorite example of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: this was actually a paper from several years ago now where it was shown that just from your likes

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: on Facebook, just from the things on which you clicked on the thumbs up button on the platform,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: not using any information, demographic information, nothing about who your friends are,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: just knowing the content that you had liked was enough to, in the aggregate, accurately predict

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: things like sexual orientation, drug and alcohol use, whether you were the child of divorced parents.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So, we live in this era where even the apparently irrelevant data that we offer about ourselves on

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: public platforms and forums often unbeknownst to us more or less acts as signature or fingerprint

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and that if you can do a join between that kind of data and allegedly anonymized data,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: you have real trouble.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So, is there hope for any kind of privacy in a world where a few likes can identify you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So, there is differential privacy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: What is differential privacy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Yeah, so differential privacy basically is an alternate much stronger notion of privacy than

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: these anonymization ideas. It's a technical definition, but the spirit of it is we compare

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to alternate worlds. So, let's suppose I'm a researcher and I want to do... There's a database

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of medical records and one of them is yours. And I want to use that database of medical records

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: to build a predictive model for some disease. So, based on people's symptoms and test results and

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the like, I want to build a model predicting the probability that people have disease. So,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: this is the type of scientific research that we would like to be allowed to continue.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And in differential privacy, you ask a very particular counterfactual question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: We basically compare two alternatives. One is when I build this model on the database of medical

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: records, including your medical record. And the other one is where I do the same exercise

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: with the same database with just your medical record removed. So, basically, it's two databases,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: one with N records in it and one with N minus one records in it. The N minus one records are

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the same and the only one that's missing in the second case is your medical record. So,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: differential privacy basically says that any harms that might come to you from the analysis

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in which your data was included are essentially nearly identical to the harms that would have

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: come to you if the same analysis had been done without your medical record included.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: So, in other words, this doesn't say that bad things cannot happen to you as a result of data

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: analysis. It just says that these bad things were going to happen to you already, even if your data

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: wasn't included. And to give a very concrete example, like we discussed at some length,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the study in the 50s that was done that established the link between smoking and lung cancer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: And we make the point that, well, if your data was used in that analysis and the world kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: knew that you were a smoker because there was no stigma associated with smoking before those

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: findings, real harm might have come to you as a result of that study that your data was included

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: in. In particular, your insurer now might have a higher posterior belief that you might have lung

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: cancer and raise your premium. So, you've suffered economic damage. But the point is that if the same

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: analysis has been done with all the other N minus one medical records and just yours missing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: the outcome would have been the same. Your data wasn't idiosyncratically

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: crucial to establishing the link between smoking and lung cancer because the link between smoking

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: and lung cancer is like a fact about the world that can be discovered with any sufficiently large

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: database of medical records. But that's a very low value of harm. Yeah. So, that's showing that

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: very little harm is done. Great. But what is the mechanism of differential privacy? So, that's the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: kind of beautiful statement of it. Well, what's the mechanism by which privacy is preserved?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Privacy is preserved. Yeah. So, it's basically by adding noise to computations. So, the basic idea

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: is that every differentially private algorithm, first of all, or every good differentially private

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: algorithm, every useful one is a probabilistic algorithm. So, it doesn't... On a given input,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: if you gave the algorithm the same input multiple times, it would give different outputs each time

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: from some distribution. And the way you achieve differential privacy algorithmically is by kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of carefully and tastefully adding noise to a computation in the right places. And to give a

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: very concrete example, if I want to compute the average of a set of numbers, the non-private way

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of doing that is to take those numbers and average them and release a numerically precise

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: value for the average. In differential privacy, you wouldn't do that. You would first compute

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: that average to numerical precisions, and then you'd add some noise to it. You'd add some kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of zero mean Gaussian or exponential noise to it so that the actual value you output is not the

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: exact mean, but it'll be close to the mean. But it'll be close... The noise that you add will sort

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: of prove that nobody can kind of reverse engineer any particular value that went into the average.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Mm-hmm. So, noise is the savior. How many algorithms can be aided by adding noise?

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Yeah. So, I'm a relatively recent member of the differential privacy community. My co-author,

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Aaron Roth, is really one of the founders of the field and has done a great deal of work. And I've

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: learned a tremendous amount working with him on it. It's a pretty grown-up field already.

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: Yeah, but now it's pretty mature. But I must admit, the first time I saw the definition of

metadata.title: Podcast: Michael Kearns: Algorithmic Fairness, Privacy & Ethics | Lex Fridman Podcast #50

body.input: differential privacy, my reaction was like, well, that is a clever definition and it's really making
